steps.body: Some numbers make only **one** rectangle. 7 tiles form a 1×7 line and nothing else — no other whole rectangle fits. Numbers like that are **prime**: their only factors are 1 and themselves. Numbers that make more than one rectangle (like 12) are **composite**.

widget.prompt: Sort each number by how many different rectangles its tiles can make.

items.feedback: 1×9 AND 3×3 — two rectangles, so 9 is composite.
1×10 AND 2×5 — more than one rectangle, so 10 is composite.

widget.missFeedback: One rectangle (just 1×n) → prime; two or more rectangles → composite.
widget.successFeedback: 7 and 13 make only a single line (prime); 9 and 10 make extra rectangles (composite).

explanationVariants: 15 = 3 × 5, so besides 1×15 it also makes a 3×5 rectangle — more than one, so composite.
15 has factors 1, 3, 5, 15 — four factors means extra rectangles, so it's composite.

options.label: Composite — it makes 1×15 AND 3×5
options.feedback: The 3×5 rectangle proves extra factors (3 and 5), so 15 is composite.

options.label: Prime — 15 is odd
options.feedback: Odd doesn't mean prime — 15 = 3 × 5. It has a 3×5 rectangle, so it's composite. (9, 21, 25 are odd composites too.)

options.label: Prime — it doesn't end in an even digit
options.feedback: The last digit doesn't decide primality. 15 splits as 3 × 5, giving a second rectangle — composite.

options.label: Neither
options.feedback: Every whole number above 1 is prime or composite. 15 has the 3×5 rectangle, so it's composite.

steps.body: The number **1 is the odd one out — neither prime nor composite.** A prime needs exactly two different factors (1 and itself); but 1's only factor is 1, so it has just ONE factor, not two. It fails the prime rule and isn't composite either. 1 sits in its own special box.

explanationVariants: A prime has exactly two different factors; 1 has only one factor (itself), so it can't be prime — or composite.
1 makes only a 1×1 square and has a single factor, failing the two-factor prime rule; it's neither.

options.label: Neither — 1 has only one factor, but a prime needs exactly two
options.feedback: Primes have two different factors (1 and themselves). 1's only factor is 1, so it's in its own box.

options.label: Prime — its only factors are 1 and itself
options.feedback: For 1, '1 and itself' are the SAME number — that's one factor, not the two a prime needs. So 1 is neither.

options.label: Composite — it's a small number
options.feedback: Composite means MORE than one rectangle; 1 makes only 1×1. Small doesn't mean composite. 1 is neither.

options.label: Both prime and composite
options.feedback: A number is prime or composite, never both — and 1 is actually NEITHER, with too few factors to be prime and too few rectangles to be composite.

widget.prompt: Tap every PRIME number (only a 1×n rectangle, exactly two factors).

hotspots.feedback: 16 makes 2×8 and 4×4 besides 1×16 — lots of rectangles, so composite, not prime.
21 = 3 × 7, so it makes a 3×7 rectangle — composite, not prime.

widget.missFeedback: A prime makes ONLY the 1×n line. If you can find any other rectangle, it's composite.
widget.successFeedback: 11, 17, and 19 make only a single line (prime); 16 and 21 have extra rectangles (composite).

predict.prompt: Can an ODD number still fail to be prime?

options.label: No — every odd number is prime

predict.reveal: Odd only means not divisible by 2 — an odd number can still split other ways, like 21 into 3 × 7. Prime demands exactly two factors.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents prime composite.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for prime composite must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines prime composite.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

explanationVariants: 9 looks prime but 9 = 3 × 3 — that 3×3 rectangle is a second option, so 9 is composite.
The trap: 9 is odd and 'feels' prime, but 3 divides it, giving a 3×3 rectangle. Composite.

widget.prompt: Which of these is NOT actually prime: 5, 9, 11, or 23?

options.label: 9 — it equals 3 × 3, so it's composite
options.feedback: 9's sneaky 3×3 rectangle gives it a third factor. The others (5, 11, 23) make only a 1×n line.
5 makes only 1×5 — a genuine prime. The composite hiding here is 9 = 3 × 3.
11 has only 1×11 — prime. Look for the one with a hidden rectangle: 9 = 3 × 3.
23 is prime (only 1×23). The odd-one-out is 9, which splits into 3 × 3.

hints: Check each number from 2 to 10 for a rectangle beyond 1×n.
2, 3, 5, 7 make only a line; 4, 6, 8, 9, 10 have extra rectangles.
Count just the ones with a single rectangle.
explanationVariants: From 2 to 10 the primes are 2, 3, 5, 7 — four of them. (4=2×2, 6=2×3, 8=2×4, 9=3×3, 10=2×5 are all composite; 1 is neither.)
Only 2, 3, 5, 7 make a single 1×n line between 2 and 10 — that's 4 primes.

widget.prompt: How many PRIME numbers are there from 2 to 10 (including 2 and 10)?

commonErrors.feedback: 5 likely counted 9 as prime — but 9 = 3 × 3 is composite. The primes 2–10 are just 2, 3, 5, 7: four.
3 may have dropped 2, the smallest prime (it makes only 1×2). The primes 2–10 are 2, 3, 5, 7 — four.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Check 2–10 one by one; count those making only a 1×n line.

takeaways: Prime = exactly two factors (1 and itself) = only a 1×n rectangle.
Composite = more than two factors = more than one rectangle.
1 is neither — it has just one factor, too few for either.

concept.body: Quick rewind. **Prime = a lonely line.** If the only rectangle a number's tiles can make is a single 1×n row, it's prime — its only factors are 1 and itself. The moment a second rectangle appears (like 3×4 for 12), the number is composite.

explanationVariants: 7 makes only 1×7 — one rectangle, so prime.
No rectangle beyond the 1×7 line fits, so 7 is prime.

options.label: Prime — only 1×7 fits
options.feedback: A single lonely line: 7 is prime.

options.label: Composite
options.feedback: 7's tiles make only the 1×7 line — no second rectangle — so it's prime, not composite.

options.label: Neither
options.feedback: Only 1 is neither. 7 makes exactly one rectangle (1×7), which makes it prime.
